module.title: Foundations of Neuroscience
module.description: Debates that framed our understanding of the brain
key_takeaways: The history of neuroscience advances through debates where both sides were often partly right and partly wrong.
Where the mind resides shifted over millennia between heart (cardiocentric) and brain (encephalocentric) views.
Settled questions can reopen when new evidence emerges — progress is incremental and self-correcting.

blocks.content: By the middle of the 18th century, the gross anatomy of the brain had been described in reasonable detail. Following Thomas Willis, work by anatomists across Europe such as Gennari, Pourfour du Petit, Rolando, Vicq-D’Azyr, and Gratiolet, gave rise to a clear and detailed picture of the brain as a complex organ with multiple distinct anatomical regions. But what was the substance making up the organ of thought, memory, and emotions? Early explorations with small, hand-held homemade microscopes (

) allowed the Dutch draper Antonie van Leeuwenhoek—who had started making his own microscopes to assess the quality of his fabrics—to examine countless biological specimens, including a cow optic nerve,

which was the first nervous tissue to be seen at high magnification. Although without methods to enhance contrast, the optic nerve must have looked fairly nondescript to van Leeuwenhoek, it was sufficient for him to remark that the nerve was not composed of a hollow tube, as had been claimed by Alcmaeon over a thousand years earlier in Greece.

This limited initial progress in brain research after the development of the first microscopes. These obstacles, which also included difficulties in tissue handling (softness, degradation) and processing (sampling for microscopy), were gradually resolved during the 19th century. First, chemical solutions, from alcohol, to balsamic concoctions, to formaldehyde (the latter being still commonly used in neuroscience research) were increasingly employed to stop tissue degradation and harden fresh tissue samples, making brain matter easier to process for microscopy
. Second, the development of a precise instrument for tissue cutting, the microtome, allowed for consistent sectioning of brain tissue that could then be mounted on glass slides
. Third, various pigments and dyes, such as carmine or cresyl violet, were found to be efficient contrasting agents, revealing for the first time the brain’s myriad building blocks
. Lastly, refinements in compound microscopes, initially invented by Robert Hooke in the mid-17th century, permitted observations of brain tissue with increasing clarity.

These would go on to be named Purkyně neurons

. It remained unclear, though, whether globules—a term first used by Gabriel Valentin, one of Purkyně’s students—and nerve fibers were connected in any way. Others, such as Robert Remak and Otto Deiters, began using other staining approaches to visualize fibers in brain and spinal cord sections. A posthumous publication from Deiters in 1865 revealed that there were in fact two types of fibers, the axis cylinder (axon) and protoplasmic processes (dendrites), that extended from what looked like cell bodies

). However, Deiters hypothesized that these processes were fused to those of other “cells.” The idea that neuronal processes fused (or anastomosed) was formalized by German anatomist Joseph von Gerlach in 1871 when he proposed that the brain is built from specialized cells with extended fibers that fused with one another, forming a giant nerve net or syncytium

. Various configurations were proposed for this syncytium: dendrites fusing with other dendrites, axons with other axons, and dendrites with axons. The reticular theory was widely accepted by biologists, even if it largely contradicted cell theory which had been formalized in 1839 by German anatomists Schwann, for animals, and Schleiden, for plants. Cell theory stated that all living organisms are made up of individual cells

, but it seemed logical to consider that the brain, capable of exceptional functions, should present an exceptional structure not dependent on individual cells doing individual things. It was natural to think that the brain, which required lightning-fast information flow across and between its various regions, could be organized as a giant net of “cells.”

blocks.content: Descartes is often credited with popularizing the idea of dualism

—the idea that most of our bodily functions and capabilities arise from our corporeal being, but that our mind, or soul, arises in an ethereal, perhaps spiritual, manner. Even hundreds of years after Descartes’ death, such ideas continue to have traction, particularly in conversations surrounding the basis of consciousness
. Somewhat ironically, in death Descartes also came to embody the idea of separation of mind and body.

blocks.content: On the first day of experiments, Bartholow had some initial success. Cortical stimulation provoked contralateral limb movements. To “develop more decided reactions,” Bartholow turned up the current, but this caused clonic spasms in Rafferty’s arm, emotional distress and crying. Rafferty then lost consciousness, during which time she exhibited convulsions. After recovering—still on this first day of experiments—Bartholow continued with stimulations, though at a lower current. A couple days later, Bartholow met again with Rafferty to continue with experiments. Her health, however, was in decline, and so the day’s activities were postponed. The following day, her condition was “decidedly worse.” She died soon afterwards, and Bartholow went on to publish a paper on his results
. This was the first documented evidence of electrical stimulation of the human brain driving motor activity, but it drew considerable ethical concerns and Bartholow publicly sought to defend himself

. It would be many years before electrical stimulation of the human brain picked back up, this time paired with resections related to epilepsy patients, pioneered by the likes of Otfrid Foerster, Harvey Cushing and Wilder Penfield.

blocks.content: In ancient Greece, the Pythogoreans were mathematicians who were into numerology, and they had a particular reverence for the number four. Subsequently, Empedocles assembled a cosmology based on tetradic categories. The universe was comprised of four fundamental elements: earth, water, air and fire. There were four cosmic entities: sky, sun, earth and sea. There are four seasons: spring, summer, winter, fall. Hippocrates applied the four seasons to ages of human beings—childhood, youth, prime old age—and linked the four elements to four fundamental humors in the body: yellow bile, black bile, phlegm, and blood

). Galen continued the Hippocratic medical practice of considering that illnesses and dispositions were caused by imbalances in the four humors, and patients were treated in a manner that sought to restore humoral balance. In practice, Galen felt that the palm of the hand was the best location to assess the balance of the humors
. Humoral theory would go on to impact medical practice for well over a thousand years.

blocks.content: In the 1950s, working at Washington University, first with Viktor Hamburger then with Stanley Cohen, Rita Levi-Montalcini made a series of breakthroughs that led to the discovery of the first-ever growth factor. Earlier, as a postgraduate student working in Turin, she had performed experiments which suggested that developing neurons required intact peripheral target tissues to survive

. At Washington University, Levi-Montalcini set out to understand what the nature of this interaction between developing neuron and target area was. By implanting tumors into chick embryos, she found that the embryos showed overabundant nerve innervations, which she thought resulted from a substance generated from the implanted tumour. Then, working with Stanly Cohen who isolated the factor, which was named Nerve Growth Factor (or NGF), she found it to be a protein capable of promoting neurite outgrowth and neuron differentiation

. Thus, consistent with Cajal’s hypothesis, there are specific external factors that neurons need to grow and develop. For this work, Rita Levi-Montalcini and Stanley Cohen were awarded the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

In his book Method of Treatment, Galen writes: "Concerning the psychic spirit [also known as animal spirits], we have clearly shown that the brain is its fount, so to speak, and that it is watered and nourished by inspiration and by the supply from the rete mirabile [also known as the retiform plexus]. Concerning the vital spirit, the demonstration has not been equally clear, yet it does not seem unlikely that it is contained in the heart and the arteries and that it too is chiefly nourished by the respiration and also the blood. And if there also is a natural spirit, this again should be contained in the liver and the veins.”

The idea being that the nature of these spirits, or pneuma, would get elaborated from one organ to the next, and the complex structure of the rete mirabile—a complex vascular mesh at the base of the brain—would allow spirits the time to develop from the vital to the psychic kind

). The only issue is that humans do not have a rete mirabile. But Galen did not have access to human tissue for dissection. He did have access to ungulates—hooved animals that possess a rete mirabile. He also mentioned that Herophilus previously described the rete mirabile, and Herophilus was thought to have dissected human tissue, so Galen may have assumed that Herophilus noted this structure in humans

. blocks.content: In contrast to the example above where an anatomical structure present in non-humans was mistakenly assigned to humans, during the heated academic debates following the release of Darwin’s On the Origins of Species, the inverse situation arose: a controversy about whether a certain brain structure was specific to humans and thus differentiated us from the rest of the animal kingdom. The year was 1858 and Richard Owen, Hunterian professor at the Royal College of Surgeons and superintendent of the British Museum, published a paper claiming that three parts of brain anatomy clearly distinguished humans from other primates. It seems likely that he was aware that Darwin’s book was about to be published and he wanted to get in front of it with a win for the anti-evolution side. In contrast to Linnaeus, Owen went so far as to put humans in an order of the phylogenetic tree all by themselves

. Owen’s claims were: 1) only in humans does the posterior part of the cerebrum (i.e., the caudal-most part of cortex) extend beyond and thus cover the cerebellum; 2) only humans have a posterior horn in their lateral ventricle; 3) only humans have a hippocampus minor (a structure now referred to as the calcar avis). The problem was that Owen—despite other important contributions to knowledge and the public dissemination of knowledge via his work at the British Museum—was wrong on each of these fronts. It seems that Owen largely based his conclusions on a belief that humans were superior to other animals, and a misreading (possibly purposefully so) of the scientific literature. Over the next years, “Darwin’s Bulldog” Thomas Huxley, then professor of General Natural History at the Government School of Mines pursued a single-minded take-down of Owen over these claims. Across several publications, Huxley and other like-minded scientists performed numerous dissections comparing human and non-human primate brains, outlining that each of Owen’s three claims were incorrect, and showing that the hippocampus minor was not unique to humans
). Though Owen dug in his heels, so much evidence accumulated against his position in a short period of time that his scientific credibility quickly declined.

blocks.content: Galen had less to work with when it came to assigning mental faculties to specific parts of the brain. As such, while he split the mental faculties into three components—imagination, reasoning, and memory—he did not propose specific brain locations where these were processed. That task would be taken up by Christian Church Fathers of the 4<sup>th</sup> century CE. They took these faculties and assigned each to a different ventricle in the brain. Since brain activity was thought to arise via pneuma or spirits (i.e., some type of air-like substance) flowing through nerves, the ventricles seemed like a good place for the pneuma to be stored and work their magic. This theory, referred to as the cell doctrine or ventricular theory, would persist in variations—some with more ventricles, some with different functions assigned to different ventricles—for the next thousand years

). In general, sensory signals were thought to be received by the most frontal ventricle. From there, pneuma would be passed onto the middle ventricle for mental processing, and then the pneuma would pass to the most anterior ventricle for mental storage.

Modern neuroanatomy can be traced back to Andreas Vesalius (1512-1564) who combined art and science in the early Renaissance to produce beautiful anatomical descriptions of the human body. His work relied on dissecting human corpses, but this was just starting to be allowed in some parts of Europe at the time. As such, sometimes Vesalius had to acquire his material in creative ways, such as getting bodies fresh from the gallows
. In his magnum opus De Humani Corporis Fabrica (1543; often referred to simply as De Fabrica;

), Vesalius provided unparalleled artistic renditions of the human brain: it’s believed the woodcut artwork was produced by students of Titian. In De Fabrica, Vesalius pinpointed numerous errors in Galen’s work, much of which likely arose since Galen did not have access to human tissue. Vesalius’ work was widely read and served as a foundation for future neuroanatomists to scrutinize and refine

. This was the case for Thomas Willis (1621-1675), who built on Vesalius’ anatomical work and combined it with findings from his clinical practice to produce the book Cerebri Anatome (1664), the most complete and detailed description of the nervous system at the time

. Willis was the first to describe the anatomy of the striatum and discovered the arterial circle at the base of the brain which bears his name to this day—the circle of Willis. Willis also coined the term neurology. Thus, by the 17<sup>th</sup> century it was clear that the brain had a complex anatomical structure, with distinct regions and connectivity patterns. This led people to start proposing specific roles for these newly described anatomical regions. Thomas Willis, for instance, proposed that common sense was housed in the striatum, imagination in the corpus collosum, and memory in the cortex

Descartes argued that the pineal gland, which lies along the midline, acted like a puppet master, directing the flow of spirits throughout the brain to control distinct functions, and acting as an interface between the physical and ethereal worlds. By reading everything he could find about anatomy and medical cases involving brain damage, he correctly deduced the general location of motor cortex and assigned roles related to executive function to the frontal lobes. The cerebrum was critical for “perception, judgement and will.

” As noted above, this was the first solid evidence that the brain housed the mind. However, in contrast to Gall, Flourens considered the cerebrum to be equipotential: “All sensations, all perceptions, and all volition occupy concurrently the same seat in these organs. ” Thus, Flourens concluded that phrenology was nonsense.

Then, in April 1861, a patient by the name of Louis Victor Leborgne came under the care of physician Paul Broca (whom we already met above in the section about trepanation). . By the time Broca saw him, Leborgne was known as “Tan,” as this was essentially the only word he could say, often repeated twice in a row. The faculty of speech reappeared as soon as the compression ceased.

Working in Berlin, neurologist Eduard Fritsch and anatomist Gustav Hitzig used electrical stimulation of cortex in dogs to identify motor cortex. Not only did they find a specific portion of cortex that could reliably drive contralateral body movements, they found that stimulating different parts of this motor cortex led to movement of different parts of the body (e.g., hind leg vs. front leg; (Figure 10)). Fritsch and Hitzig then showed that lesioning this region led to contralateral motor deficits.

blocks.content: Fritsch and Hitzig’s work was validated soon afterwards in primates by David Ferrier who was working in England. However, not everyone was convinced. A flashpoint in the debate between localizationalists and anti-localizationalists occurred at the Seventh International Medical Congress, held in 1881 in London. In attendance were 3,000 people, including clinicians and researchers, as well as political, religious and intellectual leaders

. One morning, Leopold Goltz, a German physiologist, presented one of the dogs he had worked with. Goltz claimed that, using a water pick, he had ablated motor cortex from one of the hemispheres, but the dog still moved around more or less normally. Immediately afterward, Ferrier presented one of his monkeys that had motor cortex ablated in one hemisphere. This monkey presented with hemiplegia on the contralateral side of the lesion. How could such conflicting results be assessed? Goltz and Ferrier agreed for an independent panel of experts, including a young Charles Sherrington, to euthanize the animals and examine the extent of brain damage in relation to the claims of purported lesions by Goltz and Ferrier
. In the end, it was found that Goltz’s dog had significant portions of motor cortex remaining, whereas Ferrier’s monkey had a lesion corresponding to Ferrier’s description
). Nonetheless, subsequent work would show more notable deficits in primates lacking motor cortex than in lower mammals with similar lesions, providing at least some support to Goltz.

blocks.content: By the turn of the 20<sup>th</sup> century, while researchers increasingly believed that there were cortical loci for primary sensory and motor areas, it remained controversial whether there was localization of higher brain functions. For roughly a 30-year period in the mid-20<sup>th</sup> century, Karl Lashley, an American behavioral psychologist, hunted for engrams—the physical traces of stored memories in the brain. He trained rats in mazes and memory tasks, and then lesioned various brain regions, largely in cortex, and examined the effects. He was unable to find a specific part of the brain that stored memories. This led him to conclude that unlike primary sensory cortical regions which took up defined plots of land in the brain, memories were stored everywhere (equipotentiality) and that the impact of lesions directly scaled with the size of the lesion (mass action)

blocks.content: Lashley’s conclusions on a lack of localization of function for memory processing didn’t hold for long. In the 1950s, working with Donald Hebb (a former student of Lashley’s) at the Montreal Neurological Institute, Brenda Milner began studying some of neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield’s patients who had had different brain regions resected as part of treatment for epilepsy or other neurological disorders. She noted that a couple of patients with apparent bilateral hippocampal formation resections/damage had memory-related issues. After presenting these observations at a conference, Milner and Penfield were contacted by William Scoville, an American neurosurgeon who had performed similar surgeries and had noted memory deficits in some of his patients. Milner proceeded to examine some of Scoville’s patients

, including patient H.M. (Henry Molaison), who had been having seizures since the age of 10, and severe episodes since the age of 16. By the age of 27, Molaison could no longer hold down a job and Scoville advised experimental bilateral hippocampal resection. Following the procedure, though his epilepsy was greatly reduced, Molaison could no longer form new memories (i.e., he suffered from anterograde amnesia). Milner carefully documented H.M.’s behaviors, finding that though he could not form new episodic memories, he was able to form new procedural memories (e.g., a mirror drawing task). Thus, not only was Milner able to identify the hippocampus as a critical region for the encoding of new memories
, she was also able to establish that different types of memories—e.g., episodic (“I remember what happened where”) vs. procedural (“I know how to do it”)—were stored in different brain regions.

blocks.content: Yet major issues could not be easily accounted for by electrical neuronal communication. For instance, how could electrical currents lead to inhibition in the nervous system? By the 1920s, several scientists had arrived at the conclusion that endogenous molecules were likely used by peripheral nerves. Pharmacological experiments had characterized the effects of many compounds on peripheral organs. For example, Thomas Renton Elliott published a paper in 1905 describing the effects of adrenal gland extracts on the bladder

. The relaxant effect of the extract was like that observed following stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system, which reinforced the notion that endogenous molecules could play a role at the synapse. But direct experimental evidence was lacking. This eventually gave rise to the Soups vs. Sparks debate

, with some being convinced that chemical components (soups) must mediate neurotransmission, while others firmly believed that electricity (sparks) was the only medium that could reasonably convey fast messages between neurons. This debate would be settled, in part, by studying the heart.

It occurred to me at 6.00 o’clock in the morning that during the night I had written down something important, but I was unable to decipher the scrawl. The basal ganglia of the brain are peculiarly rich in acetylcholine, the presence of which must presumably have some significance; and suggestive effects of eserine and of acetylcholine, injected into the ventricles of the brain, have been described. I take the view, however, that we need a much larger array of well authenticated facts, before we begin to theorize. It is here, especially, that we need to proceed with caution; if the principle of chemical transmission is ultimately to find a further extension to the interneuronal transmission in the brain itself, it is by patient testing of the groundwork of experimental fact, at each new step, that a safe and steady advance will be achieved. But seeing as autonomic innervations can operate on relatively slow timescales, there was resistance to the idea that chemical synaptic transmission also occurred in the CNS and at the neuromuscular junction at skeletal muscles, where fast processing is needed. The leading opponent to chemical neurotransmission in the CNS was the Australian neurophysiologist John Eccles
, who had animated public debates with Dale and others. Soon, researchers including Bernard Katz

would provide experimental evidence in support of acetylcholine being released by pre-ganglionic neurons as well as by motoneurons at the neuromuscular junction. Eventually Eccles had to recognize that chemical neurotransmission was a mechanism used throughout the peripheral nervous system

. The CNS, however, was another story, and Eccles thought of a clever hypothesis that would disprove, once and for all, the notion of chemical neurotransmission in the brain and spinal cord. blocks.content: Upon being asked why he decided to specialize in neurology, Oliver Sacks famously answered, “I became a neurologist rather than, say, a cardiologist, because there’s nothing for an intelligent man to be interested in in cardiology. The heart, I suppose, is an interesting pump, but it’s just a pump. Neurology is the only branch of medicine that could sustain a thinking man.”
In this chapter, we provide a brief survey of ideas surrounding this most fascinating of organs, told through debates that helped frame our modern understanding of the brain.

blocks.content: What did prehistorical humans know about the brain? In the mid-1860s, Paul Broca—a renowned French neurologist and anthropologist—received a skull. It was sent to him by Ephraim George Squier, an American anthropologist who had acquired the skull in Peru from a Señora Zentino, a collector of antiquities
. The skull came from an Incan burial site and had a square hole cut in it (

). To Squier, the nature of the hole suggested it had been cut while the individual was alive. He presented it to the New York Academy of Medicine, but they were unconvinced. In the western world at that time, cranial opening surgeries were rare and had very high mortality rates. Squier forwarded the skull to Broca for a second opinion. This was not the first skull recovered from an ancient site with an apparently man-made hole, but the previously observed holes had generally been attributed to traumatic injuries or posthumous rituals
. However, upon examination, Broca was convinced that this was the skull of a person who had survived at least for a few days after the procedure. Broca published his findings

, which generated immediate interest in studying trepanation—the surgical procedure of putting a hole in the skull—in ancient burial sites. For instance, Broca and his friend P. Barthélemy Prunières re-examined many skulls with holes that had previously been attributed to injuries or postmortem rituals, and concluded that many had actually been caused by trepanations in living individuals

paragraphs.content_text: What did prehistorical humans know about the brain? In the mid-1860s, Paul Broca received a trepanned Incan skull from Peru (Figure 1) and concluded the individual had survived the procedure, sparking interest in studying trepanation in ancient burial sites.

blocks.content: Subsequent examinations of ancient sites revealed that trepanations were relatively common throughout the prehistoric world, that they were performed in various different ways (
), and that they were often non-lethal

. For instance, in some Peruvian burial sites, up to 30% of skulls exhibit trepanation, with a survival rate—as evidenced by osteoclastic activity, remodeling, and healing around the trepanned site—of over 80%

. Why were such holes made? Without a written record it’s impossible to say with certainty, but it’s likely the reasons were either superstitious, ritualistic, or medical. Possible evidence for a superstitious or ritualistic basis for trepanations comes from a Copper Age burial site in what is now Southern Russia

. In contrast to all other trepanned skulls found in prehistorical sites throughout the world, skulls from these sites predominantly exhibit trepanned holes located over the midline, near the obelion. The consistency of the hole location, and the fact that this location is considered to be a very dangerous spot to open (even the Hippocratic writings warn to avoid trepanation over sutures
), suggests such procedures were possibly performed in service of some type of ritual
. As possible evidence for medical-related trepanations, some trepanation sites appear to be adjacent to trauma sites, suggesting the trauma precipitated the trepanation
. Nowadays, the vast majority of trepanations are performed in hospitals as part of modern medical procedures, though certain, albeit rare occult trepanation rituals persist

paragraphs.content_text: Trepanations were relatively common throughout the prehistoric world (Figure 2), performed in various ways and often non-lethal, with survival rates over 80% at some Peruvian sites. The reasons were likely superstitious, ritualistic, or medical.

blocks.content: Writing arose over 5,000 years ago in Sumeria and Egypt. From these early texts we gain an understanding about ancient ideas surrounding the brain. For instance, Egyptians believed that Thoth, a bird-like god—who is said to have created writing—revealed all medical knowledge via a secret book visible only to magician-priests. Healing temples arose that were named after Imhotep, a chancellor and high priest who was believed to have written numerous medical wisdom texts. The Egyptians believed that the heart was the most important organ and was connected to other parts of the body by various channels (e.g., veins, arteries, tendons)

. The heart was believed to record good and evil deeds (perhaps an early analogy of memory), and after death it was thought to be weighed, assigning the deceased to either heaven or fated to a crocodile-like creature called the Devourer. For those wealthy or fortunate enough to be embalmed or mummified after death, the brain was removed via the nostrils and discarded, unlike other organs that were stored in jars

paragraphs.content_text: Writing arose over 5,000 years ago in Sumeria and Egypt. The Egyptians believed the heart was the most important organ, recording good and evil deeds, while the brain was removed and discarded during mummification.

blocks.content: The most ancient text mentioning the brain dates to about 1,600 BCE and is written in hieroglyphs. It’s a copy of a surgical treatise originally written some 1,400 years earlier
and is known as the Edwin Smith papyrus (

), named after the American Egyptologist who purchased it in 1862 from an antiquities dealer near Luxor. This papyrus describes 48 cases, mostly of severe physical traumas, along with treatment recommendations. Many of the cases involve head injuries, including the now famous case n. 20 which describes a man with a hole in his skull—likely the result of a blow to the head sustained on the battlefield—that exposed the cortical surface of his brain (

). The case description, titled Instructions concerning a wound in his temple, penetrating to the bone, (and) perforating his temporal bone, recounts the effects of applying pressure on the exposed brain: “… if thou puttest thy finger on the mouth of the wound… he shudder exceedingly.” However, instead of recommending a surgical procedure, the suggested treatment was, “Now when thou findest that man speechless, his [relief] shall be sitting; soften his head with grease, (and) pour [milk] into both his ears.”

paragraphs.content_text: The most ancient text mentioning the brain (~1,600 BCE) is the Edwin Smith papyrus (Figure 3), a surgical treatise describing 48 cases. Case 20 (Figure 4) describes a skull wound exposing the brain, noting that pressure on it made the patient shudder.

blocks.content: Other early texts indicate that, like the Egyptians, ancient Mesopotamian, Indian and Chinese thinkers also tended to consider the heart as the principle organ of the mind
. That being said, some relatively correct functions were assigned to the brain early on: the Edwin Smith Papyrus relates damage to one side of the head leading to hemiplegia
(paralysis on the other side of the body); the Indian Charaka Samhita indicates that head issues can lead to facial paralysis and muteness

paragraphs.content_text: Like the Egyptians, ancient Mesopotamian, Indian and Chinese thinkers tended to consider the heart the principal organ of the mind, though some correct brain functions were noted early, such as head damage leading to contralateral paralysis.

blocks.content: It wasn’t until ancient Greece that a serious debate arose about whether the heart was truly the seat of the mind, or if instead it was the brain

. In fact, ideas about the seat of the mind were diverse in ancient Greece: “Whereas Empedocles placed the seat of the soul in the blood, Parmenides and Epicurus in the chest, Strato between the eyebrows, Democritus and Plato in the head as a whole, others placed it in the meninges and Herophilus in the ventricles of the brain.”
Alcmaeon, an early proponent of animal dissections for gaining anatomical insights, wrote that “a man smelled with his nostrils as he drew breath up to the brain.”

paragraphs.content_text: It was not until ancient Greece that a serious debate arose about whether the heart or the brain was the seat of the mind. Views were diverse, with thinkers placing the soul in the blood, chest, head, meninges, or ventricles.

blocks.content: In 5<sup>th</sup> century BCE, Hippocrates of Cos and his followers considered the brain to be the seat of intelligence and consciousness, believed the brain controlled many bodily functions, and thought the brain was at the root of what are now considered neurological disorders and mental illnesses
. For example, the Hippocratic writings instructed that it is “the brain which permits the perception of hearing, vision and smell; from those memory and intuition arise.”

Hippocratic medicine was based on observation, with little room for the magical or the sacred in guiding understanding of the body’s functions and dysfunctions, though they were heavily influenced by humoral theory. However, neuroanatomy, beyond some basic knowledge derived from a small number of animal dissections, was not viewed as important by Hippocrates.

paragraphs.content_text: In the 5th century BCE, Hippocrates of Cos and his followers considered the brain the seat of intelligence and consciousness and the root of neurological and mental disorders, basing their medicine on observation rather than the magical or sacred.

blocks.content: Plato was another influential Greek thinker who held an encephalocentric view. For example, he relays this from Socrates: “…[I]t is the brain that conveys sensations like hearing, seeing and smelling, so that memory and opinion are produced and, once they had firmly settled [in our mind], knowledge is generated in such way.”
Much like Democritus before him, Plato argued for a triune, or tripartite, soul

: the head or brain contained an immortal, rational soul; the chest contained a mortal soul that was the source of our feelings; the gut region contained the soul of nourishment and passions. One reason Plato favoured the head as the seat of the mind was for idealistic reasons: the cosmos was a sphere, and the earth was a sphere at the center of the cosmos, and so it made sense that our most divine part, our mind/soul, would be located in our most spherical structure, our head

paragraphs.content_text: Plato held an encephalocentric view, relaying from Socrates that the brain conveys sensation and generates knowledge. He argued for a tripartite soul, favouring the head partly for idealistic reasons: it was our most spherical, and thus most divine, structure.

blocks.content: In contrast to Plato, his pupil Aristotle held a cardiocentric point of view. Aristotle, who performed comparative anatomical analyses in several animal species, also split the soul into three components, but he used these to separate man from plants and other animals. He argued that all organisms have a vegetative/nourishing soul, all animals possess a sensitive, motor soul, but only humans possess an immaterial intellectual soul (Alcmaeon had argued earlier that understanding is what separated humans from other animals)
. Aristotle placed the seat of these souls in the heart

. In part, he argued for a cardiocentric view because he considered the heart to be warm, and thus vital, whereas he thought the brain was cold—Galen would test this a few hundred years later and find that the brain was warm. Aristotle argued that the brain served to cool down the heart, going so far as to posit that we sleep at the end of the day since the brain’s cooling abilities were insufficient:

“For, as has been observed elsewhere, sleep comes on when the corporeal element [in the ‘evaporation’] conveyed upwards by the hot, along the veins, to the head. But when that which has been thus carried up can no longer ascend, but is too great in quantity [to do so], it forces the hot back again and flows downwards. Hence it is that men sink down [as they do in sleep] when the heat which tends to keep them erect (man alone, among animals, being naturally erect) is withdrawn; and this, when it befalls them, causes unconsciousness, and afterwards phantasy.<sup class="citation-ref" data-ref="16">16</sup>”

paragraphs.content_text: In contrast to Plato, his pupil Aristotle held a cardiocentric view, placing the seat of the soul in the heart, which he considered warm and vital, while thinking the brain was cold and served only to cool the heart — even attributing sleep to the brain’s insufficient cooling.

blocks.content: Dissections of the human brain and body only truly began with Herophilus (335-280 BCE) and Erasistratus (304-250 BCE), when, for a brief period of time, studying human cadavers was permitted at the Alexandria School of Medicine in Egypt

. By dissecting bodies of criminals executed at the Ptolemean court, these Greek physicians pioneered the field of human anatomy and provided the first descriptions of the cerebrum, the cerebellum, and the cerebral ventricles in the human brain. Herophilus and Erasistratus were the first to define nerves, and showed that they could be traced back to the brain and the spinal cord
. At one point, Erasistratus argued that the meninges housed the mind

paragraphs.content_text: Human dissection truly began with Herophilus and Erasistratus at the Alexandria School of Medicine, who pioneered human anatomy, gave the first descriptions of the cerebrum, cerebellum, and ventricles, and were the first to define nerves and trace them to the brain and spinal cord.

blocks.content: The works of Herophilus and Erasistratus are not extant, but were passed down by the works of others, including Galen (129-216 CE), who in turn argued strongly in favour of the brain as the seat of the mind. After Hippocrates, Galen, a Greek physician working in Rome, had the most significant impact on medicine. This was in part because, like Hippocrates, he advocated for direct observation and against superstition. He served as the personal physician to several emperors, including Marcus Aurelius
. Based on animal dissections, he described cranial and peripheral nerves, and showed that the brain and spinal cord were the source of nerves

. Additionally, he explored subcortical structures and described cerebral ventricles more extensively than his predecessors. However, by Galen’s time dissections on human cadavers were no longer allowed, which limited his insights into human neuroanatomy.

paragraphs.content_text: Galen (129-216 CE) argued strongly for the brain as the seat of the mind and, after Hippocrates, had the greatest impact on medicine. Based on animal dissections, he described cranial and peripheral nerves and the ventricles, though a ban on human dissection limited his neuroanatomy.

blocks.content: Despite Galen arguing that the mind arose in the parenchyma, or brain tissue, much attention would subsequently be given to the ventricles as possible nodes of the mind (as will be described in detail in the next section). However, it wasn’t until the 1800s that Marie Pierre Jean Flourens, in his efforts to disprove phrenology (see more on this below as well), resected various brain regions, largely from rabbits and pigeons, and showed somewhat specific behavioral impacts. He found that removing the cerebrum appeared to impair sensory perception and judgement, while removing the cerebellum seemed to impair equilibrium and coordination. Thus Flourens, despite remaining adamant that there was no localization of function within the cerebrum, firmly placed the mind in the brain

paragraphs.content_text: After Galen, attention turned to the ventricles as possible seats of the mind. In the 1800s, Flourens resected brain regions in rabbits and pigeons, showing the cerebrum affected perception and judgement and the cerebellum affected coordination — firmly placing the mind in the brain.

images.caption: Medieval cell doctrine with five cells arranged in a linear sequence by the German Dominican friar and historian Johann Lindner (1440–1524), as part of notes for Albertus Magnus’s Parvulus philosophiae naturalis. Source: Lindner (1472–1474). Courtesy of the Wellcome Library, London. Figure legend from Lanska, 2024, Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Neuroscience.

Medieval cell doctrine with five cells arranged in a nonlinear sequence (ca. 1300), illumination on parchment by an unknown English miniaturist. The vermis (worm) guards the entrance of the posterior cell. Source: University Library, Cambridge, ms Gr.g.1.1; Web Gallery of Art. Figure legend from Lanska, 2024, Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Neuroscience.

The medieval cell doctrine according to Albertus Magnus, as presented in the first printed example of this doctrine, which appeared in Philosophia pauperum, sive Philosophia naturalis [Philosophy for the simple, or Natural philosophy] in 1490 (an earlier edition of this incunabulum from 1485 was not illustrated). In discussing the soul (De anima), Albertus Magnus partitioned cognitive abilities into three cells or ventricles, with the common sense (sensus communis) and imagination (imaginatio) in the first ventricle, the imaginative faculty (imaginativa) and extimativa (sic, judgment) in the second, and finally memory (memorativa) and the control of motion (membro motiva) in the third. Courtesy of the U.S. National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, Maryland, United States. Figure edited by Douglas J. Lanska. Figure legend from Lanska, 2024, Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Neuroscience.

The medieval cell doctrine combined with elementary anatomy from Johannes Peyligk (1474–1522) from 1499. The woodcut shows a schematic layout of the ventricular system viewed from the side (although the head is actually only turned about 45 degrees), with both lateral ventricles, the third ventricle, and the fourth ventricle all depicted. Courtesy of the Herzog August Bibliothek in Wolfenbüttel, Germany. Figure edited by Douglas J. Lanska. Figure legend from Lanska, 2024, Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Neuroscience.

Other depictions of the ventricular system from Peyligk (1499). (a) Top: Ventricular system from above, visualized through the skull and brain and (b) bottom: Ventricular system with drainage pathways to the pituitary. Courtesy of the Herzog August Bibliothek in Wolfenbüttel, Germany. Figures edited by Douglas J. Lanska. Figure legend from Lanska, 2024, Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Neuroscience.

Anatomy of the head and brain as depicted in a woodcut by German physician, philosopher, and theologian Magnus Hundt (1449–1519) in 1501. Note the two round structures at the bridge of the nose. These represent the olfactory bulbs. They project and appear to join in a network at the base of the brain (the mythical rete mirabile). Also present are projections from the eyes, tongue, and body to three cavities in a band above the eyes and ears; this is a representation of the medieval cell doctrine showing the three cells or ventricles with functional divisions depicted schematically by divisional lines in each of the ventricles. Above this are schematic depictions of the cranial sutures and the sequential tissues external to the skull. Courtesy of the Wellcome Library, London. Figure edited by Douglas J. Lanska. Figure legend from Lanska, 2024, Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Neuroscience.

The medieval cell doctrine according to Italian philosopher and physician Alessandro Achillini (1463/1461–1512) from Opusculum perutile de cognitione animae et eius potentiis Augustini de Anchona cum quadam questione Prosperi de Regio (1503). Courtesy of the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Roma [National Central Library, Rome], Italy. Figure edited by Douglas J. Lanska. Figure legend from Lanska, 2024, Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Neuroscience.

Illustration of the medieval cell doctrine from the encyclopedic compilation Margarita philosophica (The Pearl of Wisdom, or The Philosophical Pearl) by German Carthusian monk and humanist writer Gregor Reisch (ca. 1467–1525). The skull is cut away in a band to allow viewing of the brain and the ventricular system within it, along with the specific cognitive faculties localized to each of the ventricles. The curlicues around the ventricles are meant to portray the sulci of the cerebral cortex. The woodcut shown was used in the authorized editions in 1503, March 1504, February 1508, 1517, 1536, and 1583. Courtesy of the University of Iowa Libraries, Iowa City, Iowa (Reisch, 1504). Figure edited by Douglas J. Lanska. Figure legend from Lanska, 2024, Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Neuroscience.

Anatomy of the head and brain as depicted in a woodcut by Johannes Dryander (1500–1560) in 1537. This image was clearly derived from the one by Magnus Hundt in 1501. It continues the same medieval fictions, while resolving some problems with Hundt’s figure and creating some new problems and misunderstandings. It is a striking example of the persistence of erroneous medieval ideas, despite the work of other pre-Vesalian anatomists, such as Jacopo Berengario da Carpi (1460–1530), in the intervening years. Nevertheless, this image also shows a dramatic improvement in realism (naturalism), representation of light and shadow, and single-point linear perspective represented in woodcuts over that period. Courtesy of the U.S. National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, Maryland, United States. Figure edited by Douglas J. Lanska. Figure legend from Lanska, 2024, Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Neuroscience.

English physician Robert Fludd’s scheme for the medieval cell doctrine (Fludd, 1619). See text for details. Courtesy of the Bibliothèque municipale de Lyon [Lyon Public Library], Lyon, France. Figure edited by Douglas J. Lanska. Figure legend from Lanska, 2024, Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Neuroscience.
